publishFields.body:
As documentation grows, it becomes harder to understand how a decision connects to concepts and work—not just where it was written.

I built a public version of AI Systems Atlas to explore this problem.

It parses README and dev-plan Markdown through a Remark AST to create document, section, concept, and task nodes. Relationships backed by source paths and line references are kept separate from connections used for screen composition. The result can be explored through constellation, nebula, and orbit views built with TypeScript, React, and Three.js.

The public demo is a read-only static snapshot with no login. Markdown import and repository synchronization are available in the local app.

Demo: https://ai-systems-atlas.vercel.app/?scope=corpus&view=constellation
GitHub: https://github.com/coreline-ai/memory_node_graph
License: MIT

When working with technical documentation, which feels more lacking in practice: understanding the full context or tracing claims back to their sources?

summary.oneSentence: AI Systems Atlas explores how technical documents, concepts, and tasks connect while preserving source-level evidence.
summary.shortIntro: As documentation grows, understanding how a decision connects to concepts and work becomes harder than simply finding where it was written.

publishFields.firstComment:
Hi Product Hunt — I built AI Systems Atlas because long collections of READMEs and development plans make it difficult to see how concepts, decisions, and tasks connect.

The app parses Markdown with an AST, keeps source-backed relationships separate, and renders the result as constellation, nebula, and orbit views in Three.js. The public demo is read-only and works without signup, and the source is available under the MIT license.

I would especially value feedback on two questions:

1. Can you understand what to do within the first 30 seconds?
2. Does the source evidence make each relationship feel trustworthy?

Current limits: the live demo is a read-only static snapshot. Importing Markdown or syncing repositories requires the local app, which runs on Node.js 22.13+.

Thanks for trying it. Concrete feedback on the first confusing step would help shape the next iteration.
